speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Specifically, clause 3(b) of the Bill amends the NPF Act to allow NPF funds to be used to anchor quality investments in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Investment promotion has been a cornerstone of Singapore’s economic growth over the years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The Government quickly recognised that rapid industrialisation and investment from multinational enterprises (MNEs) were needed to provide jobs for large numbers of unemployed workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: To accelerate the pace of industrialisation and inflow of investments, Dr Goh Keng Swee established the Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB) in 1961 to attract MNEs to Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The Government built on the initial momentum to establish Singapore as a credible location for higher-value and more advanced economic activities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: We built up key infrastructure, we set aside industrial land and developed our utilities, transport and communications networks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: We also invested in other intangible fundamentals – our operating software and the skills of our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: We developed our workers, equipping them with skills for the new jobs that would come.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: We also fostered strong tripartite relations as a foundation for economic stability and growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: We put in place a strong governance and legal framework, so that investors would have the confidence that their business operations and assets would be protected, contracts would be honoured and there is strong rule of law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: With these conditions in place, we attracted MNEs, such as Texas Instruments, Philips and Panasonic, previously known as Matsushita, to set up in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: They brought with them production capabilities and management know-how.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Local companies that supplied to these MNEs benefited as they built up capabilities and gained access to the global market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Similarly, workers employed by these MNEs and their local suppliers benefited.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: They were able to earn a stable income and acquired valuable skills to progress in their careers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Through these investments, we grew our economy and created employment opportunities for Singaporeans over the years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Today, our economy is in a stronger position.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Singapore is a regional and global hub for many MNEs and a leading international financial centre.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: We are a global trading hub, with strengths in transportation and logistics, anchored by our world-class air and sea ports.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: We also have a vibrant manufacturing sector with key segments like electronics, chemicals and biomedical science.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: These generate good jobs for our people and deepen the expertise and sophistication of our economy, which, in turn, enhance Singapore’s competitiveness against other cities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: But we cannot take this for granted, as nothing in our story of survival and success is pre-ordained or guaranteed to last forever.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: We know that the external environment has become more challenging and competition for investments is increasing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: With the Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS 2.0) initiative, we have less scope to use tax incentives as a tool to attract new investments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: At the same time, countries are intensifying their efforts to attract new investments, particularly in strategic sectors, such as semiconductors and biomedical manufacturing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Several countries have already announced generous incentives to anchor manufacturing activities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The US CHIPS and Science Act sets aside S$69 billion to support semiconductor manufacturing, R&D and workforce development.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: India has similarly announced a S$13 billion package to attract investments in semiconductor manufacturing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: We will not be able to, nor should we try to, outbid these major economies in terms of spending.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: But we will certainly have to do more to ensure that Singapore remains competitive and relevant on the global stage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: We must, therefore, double down on our productivity efforts and ensure that our workforce remains highly skilled and competitive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Only then can we remain attractive to foreign investors, grow strong local companies that can do well in domestic and overseas markets and ensure that Singapore remains top-of-mind as a choice destination for investments and talent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: We are setting aside funds when we can, to ensure that we have the resources ready to anchor new investments when there are opportunities to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: This is crucial because MNEs make their investment decisions based on business and investment cycles, which may not align neatly with funding mechanisms bound by the terms of Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: This Bill will amend the NPF Act to effect the changes announced at Budget this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: If Parliament approves this Bill, funds from the NPF can be used to support all three prongs of Singapore’s economic growth strategy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: We will continue to tap on the NPF to support local enterprises to improve productivity and generate greater value.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: One scheme that the NPF has supported is the Construction Productivity and Capability Fund (CPCF).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: It offers incentives to help firms adopt productive technology and develop their workforce to raise productivity in the construction sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: We also want to continue investing in CET and lifelong learning to further strengthen our human capital.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: It can also support efforts by MNEs to train and upskill local workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: As I explained earlier in my speech, attracting MNEs to Singapore will benefit our local companies as they can access opportunities to get more contracts, enhance their capabilities, including upskilling of workers and developing strong track records, to support their overseas expansion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: This is how we ensure that each new investment we bring in strengthens the vibrancy of our economy, enhances our competitiveness and, ultimately, benefits Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, geopolitical and economic rivalry between the United States and China – two of the world’s largest economies and Singapore’s top trading partners – may threaten this investment trend.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In Deputy Prime Minister Wong’s Budget speech earlier in February this year, he mentioned that "The geopolitical context has shifted greatly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Great power contestation has intensified, most notably between the US and China." Due to this, MNEs are reconfiguring supply chains, at times, moving away from the most cost-efficient configurations to a more robust supply chain that takes these geopolitical risks into serious consideration.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There is a trend of MNEs relocating to safer locations to avoid geopolitical conflicts.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He mentioned, "All this is setting off a dangerous dynamic towards greater economic nationalism and protectionism around the world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Governments are stumping out more aggressive support, in the form of tax breaks and subsidies, to anchor strategic industries." In addition to the increased economic nationalism and protectionism around the world, the higher inflation rates, higher interest rates, higher borrowing cost and cost-of-capital, the manpower crunch, our higher wages and even higher dormitory cost and rental market continue to increase the cost of doing business in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our strong currency also means Singapore-based businesses are finding it harder to compete through cost in the global market.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Furthermore, additional headwinds, such as the impending increase in carbon tax and the implementation of the BEPS 2.0 initiative, may add even more costs to doing business in Singapore, something which Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat mentioned earlier, too.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The US and other countries are rolling out aggressive tax breaks and subsidies to attract investments, such as the CHIPS and Science Act in the US, to build up their industries and revitalise their domestic manufacturing, competing with Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat mentions that other countries like India are also intensifying their investment promotion.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: BEPS2.0 tax equalisation reduces Singapore’s investment attraction capabilities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, the best way to deal with the geopolitical uncertainty, the increased competition and the cost pressures is for Singapore to continue to be a trusted investment destination, to remain open and to boost the long-term productivity and global competitiveness of our enterprises.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, I am in support of the amendments to the NPF Bill.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I have three points of clarification to make.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And how do we prevent it from being abused?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thirdly, given that the Industry Transformation Map (ITM) is funded through NPF, what is the status and progress of ITM 2.0 or the ITM refresh?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Allow me to elaborate more on the first point.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The NPF was established in 2010 to support a wide range of measures for businesses to improve productivity and continue to educate and train workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Now, NPF’s scope is expanded to include investment promotion.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The amendment allows the fund to be used for grants to enterprises for Singapore investments and economic activities which are aimed to develop the economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Are there specific industries or critical or novel technology strands that we are targeting?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The reason for the question is because while $4 billion is a large sum of money, it pales in comparison with the resources other countries have and, hence, we must be selective and be very clear on the capabilities that we want to develop which leverage on our infrastructure, geopolitical positioning and, most importantly, the capabilities of our workforce and the added capabilities that we want to develop for our workforce.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That investment promotion alone is 2.5 times the size of our NPF top-up!

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As NPF is also used to continue to educate and train our workers, how do we ensure the NPF is utilised and distributed fairly across educating and training workers to improving productivity and investment promotion?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we find the right balance so that we do not overinvest in one at the expense of others?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the $4 billion  top-up to the NPF, what is the expected duration that the fund will last for and what are the specific targets that we want to achieve for these funds?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The example on the funding support from Germany for Intel’s new factory shows that our NPF resource is quite limited when compared to others.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we expand the scope of the NPF to anchor more quality investments in Singapore, how do we ensure that the funds are effectively used by businesses to drive real productivity, productivity improvements that will lower the cost of doing business in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we ensure that the funds drive a real reduction in the operating cost of businesses so that we can remain globally competitive?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we link funding support for businesses with tangible, proven improvement to business performance?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With our limited funds, we must ensure that every single dollar is effectively used at driving transformation for our businesses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we ensure the NPF is effectively used, we must also ensure that it is not abused.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lim made 400 fraudulent claims involving fictitious purchases of software made by the applicant companies from a pool of six shell vendor companies.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In 2020, Ng Cheow Chai, who runs two machinery companies, helped 83 businesses submit fraudulent claims to the Productivity and Innovation Credit (PIC) scheme seeking payouts of $2.7 million between March 2013 and July 2016.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He pleaded guilty to 57 income tax charges involving more than $1.4 million in cash payouts and bonuses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In 2018, S Chandran admitted to submitting $1 million in fake PIC claims.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These three cases are just some of the cases involving fraudulent claims drawing down from the NPF.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we want to make it easy for businesses to utilise NPF to improve their productivity and remain competitive, we must also ensure that the system is robust and cannot be abused by unscrupulous individuals.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Moreover, these sectors demonstrated enhanced productivity, growing by 4% annually between 2016 and 2022, compared to the economy's 3.5%.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Minister Gan also discussed the impending ITM 2025 refresh, designed to incorporate pandemic-induced lessons and address emergent priorities like sustainability and economic resilience.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond the emerging priorities of learnings from the pandemic and greater economic resilience seen in 2023 during the Budget debates, are the ITM and Job transformation Map (JTM) considering the impact of generative AI?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can I also request that the JTM and ITM refresh consider strongly promoting job redesign for the soon-to-be seniors, so that future seniors who are now digitally literate and exposed to digital technologies will have the opportunity for other job roles in the future which are beyond the manual labour-intensive jobs, such as cleaning?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I support the thrust of this expanded objective and, by extension, the Bill, I have some reservations about this wider coverage as to whether it may inadvertently lead to a dilution in the purposes of the Fund, which would, in turn, be detrimental to the ultimate goal of producing sustainable growth in the longer run.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the amendment likewise adds the qualifier that the Fund may be applied to the "promotion of   investment   economic activities in Singapore".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my view, this is relatively expansive language.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Were this Bill to pass, investments by the NPF would no longer be limited to just financing for productivity enhancement or continuing education as they currently are, but investments in general, so long as they contribute towards economic development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But would this mean that the Fund could be directed towards crude capital accumulation, such as the purchasing of capital equipment or funding of factory construction?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What about infrastructure projects, like a new Changi Terminal, which could otherwise be financed by other instruments, such as SINGA bonds?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By a similar token, what are allowable promotions for economic activities?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Would it include, for instance, marketing sports events, such as the Singapore Rugby Sevens, although I would be happy if they were to do so, or the Grand Prix, Singapore Art Week or Singapore Food Festival?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What about Taylor Swift and Jackie Cheung concerts?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, having taken over the Sports Hub, these now certainly qualify as "economic activities" within the purview of the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my view, these investments fall well outside the scope of productivity-enhancing activities and, hence, should not qualify for NPF grants.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Allowing them, as well-meaning as it might be, would subvert the original objectives of the NPF.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And while one may make a case for supporting growth at all costs, I believe that this is similarly wrong-headed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We already know how to rudely drive growth: crank up capital expenditure, unfortunately, to the detriment often of both labour income and productivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, this has been a consistent criticism of Singapore's growth model during its rapid-growth phase from the 1960s through the 1990s and was the impetus for the menagerie of productivity campaigns and bodies that, alas, saw largely a continuation of our nation's relatively anaemic productivity gains, at least relative to our headline growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, while it is tempting for us to look to bolstering growth from tried-and-tested tools, such as building up yet more of our already-intensive capital stock, we must surely resist, because it is clear that returns to ploughing further resources into investment are already hitting diminishing returns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, doing so would undermine the very purpose of the Fund, which is to elevate productivity and not investment per se.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am on the record for supporting that initiative and continue to do so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But just as important to productivity, especially economy-wide productivity, is the need to not just boost innovation but also the assimilation and deployment of said innovation throughout firms in the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And while automation and digitalisation were at the forefront of the previous wave of productivity increments, the next one is far more likely to be driven by artificial intelligence (AI) and robotisation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This topic is not unfamiliar to this House.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Members have asked about the rollout of AI in Singapore, including by my hon friend Ms He Ting Ru, on how our local workforce will meet demand for AI skills, by the hon Members Desmond Choo and Melvin Yong on incorporating AI into the school curriculum and Government services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And Ms He, along with Ms Tin Pei Ling, have also posed questions about Government oversight of AI, underscoring the common fear that, absent robust regulation, AI may run amok.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: AI is but the latest example of a general-purpose technology, for which large-language models and generative AIs, such as ChatGPT, are the latest – albeit most impressive – iteration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: General-purpose technologies are technologies that permeate every aspect of daily life, gradually improving over time, while holding the tantalising ability to spawn further innovation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Steam, electricity and information and communications technology (ICT) are earlier examples.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These earlier waves of general-purpose technologies found their way into the economy at a slower rate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the pace of adoption has accelerated over time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The steam engine only became widely used in Britain after 100 years and needed another quarter-century before making it across Europe.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Electrification required about a half-century to become ubiquitous, while computers and the Internet took at least a generation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Smartphones have spread much more rapidly, finding their way into the hands of even those in the remotest parts of Asia and Africa in a little more than a decade.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, even when compared to companies at the forefront of Web 2.0, such as Facebook and Twitter – today Meta and X – both of which gathered a million users after only a year or two.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And unlike early general-purpose technologies, AI appears to be threatening the top, rather than the bottom of the distribution of human capabilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Up till now, the spectre of technological progress had often come for the blue-collar job.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the late 18th century, textile workers displaced by the steam-powered looms followed the apocryphal example of the apprentice Ned Ludd, smashing the machines that replaced them and thereby earning the derisory moniker "Luddite", a term we still use today to refer to technophobes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The accelerated adoption of automated-switching telephones after the Second World War made the services of manual switchboard operators redundant, while more recently, the personal computer and smart phone replaced the stenographer and secretary, white-collar functions requiring only modest skills and training.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, while the computer scientists that design algorithms for AI and other machine learning models will still likely find themselves relevant in an AI-driven economy, a great many others will find themselves less lucky.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Pair AI with advances in robotics that have become ever-better at fine modus and gross motor functions, from piecing together microchips to navigating military obstacle courses to driving cars and trucks and it becomes difficult to imagine what sort of jobs are not immune to the threat from this newest wave of general-purpose technology.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Taken together, our economy will need to transform itself as never before to adapt to these changes faster than ever before.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On the benefits side, we might expect that the general-purpose technology could provide a boost to productivity and, more generally, welfare.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Workers whose jobs are destroyed – think horse-breeders and carriage-makers after the car became widespread or candle and lantern makers after the advent of the light bulb – will see a downward spiral in incomes, employability and, eventually, economic security.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There will be winners – think IBM and Microsoft after the invention of the personal computer, or Amazon and Google following the Internet revolution – as well as losers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If history is any guide, the leaps made in the earlier stages after the introduction of a new technology will peter out over time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After the initial disruption, completely new applications, once inconceivable to contemporaries, would find their way into common use.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The producers of "Gone with the Wind" and "Wizard of Oz" could scarcely have imagined that, one day, their industry would become one where actors would perform in front of a green screen, wired up, alongside computer-generated co-stars, all digitally delivered and enjoyed predominantly not in the cinemas but at home.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Spreadsheets may have been expected to render accountants irrelevant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But what that meant was that tedious bookkeeping functions now came to occupy less time of our accounting professionals, allowing them to focus on higher-order, value-added tasks like balance-sheet analysis and forecasting, along with advisory functions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: AI is likely to do the same, but supercharged.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Along with these novel uses, new jobs will be created.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Horseshoe blacksmiths became old-school auto mechanics, who have now become diagnostic operators who predominantly replace circuit boards in cars.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, almost by definition, we cannot conceive of the sort of labour needs that an AI-cum-robotics-driven future economy may demand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But it is likely to be in areas that are uniquely human.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Jobs that require an interpersonal touch, such as counseling and care, are in less danger; as are manual, physical roles like welding, electrical wiring, haircuts, massages that robots perhaps can replicate, but, for now at least, are not quite able to do so as quickly and efficiently – or enjoyably.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps, more importantly, AI can augment our existing work, especially in the creative professions, so long as we are able to leverage AI to customise goods and service offerings, thereby expanding both the size and scope of the market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For example, a beauty advisor for cosmetics may be able to use AI to scan a customer's face, offer recommendations suited for the individual, cross-referenced to their historical purchases and preferences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At one level, this may reduce the work of any given advisor, but if it reduces the time required for the advisor to serve a customer, it could drum up additional business instead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The AI rollout has already resulted in firms with greater AI exposure to run ahead of those with less.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Once these transformations occur, we will likely be able to reap the net benefits of AI for our economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The world has seen a dramatic slowing of productivity worldwide after the 2007 Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, as far back as the 1980s, Nobel Prize winner Robert Solow commented that one could see the IT revolution everywhere, except in the productivity statistics.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That productivity boost eventually arrived around a decade or two later and bumped up productivity for a decade-and-a-half, at least until the crisis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This then is the fundamental promise of the AI revolution – a revitalisation of our nation's productivity and growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: How soon we get there is unclear, as are the sorts of disruptions that will occur along the way, but it is now incumbent on the Government, working hand in hand with our private sector, to help our companies, both large and small, to utilise AI in their business and operations and to help our workers get comfortable working with AI as they go about their work day.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This should be a major imperative for our nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is important that we remember that technology adoption is neither inevitable nor automatic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Rather, efforts must be directed specifically to domestic investments and technology adoption as well as R&D tailored towards that purpose.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is why, in my view, the language of the Bill should, as far as possible, be clearly limited to productivity-enhancing investments because it will ensure that the dollars in NPF are channelled towards this specific purpose.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, this is not, nor should it be, limited to companies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Thankfully, the original Act already allows for the funding of continuing education, training, research and scholarships, all of which may be directed towards human capital accumulation in support of raising productivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is imperative, however, that such research and training opportunities be available to the typical worker and SME, rather than being limited to just highly-skilled, so-called "knowledge workers" or large multinationals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is the only way to ensure that the AI revolution becomes infused into the broad fabric of our economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Over the next decade or so, the NFP, working through these Government intermediaries, should be applied as much as possible towards helping our local companies and people become fully AI-enabled.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More generally, we need to allow AI to fully permeate our companies and workers to become an invention that fosters itself, new methods of invention and new ways of going about doing things.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When that eventually occurs, the productivity gains that have so far eluded us may perhaps finally find fruition.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It is now my pleasure to call on hon Member, Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim, to make her inaugural speech in Parliament.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The fund was set up in 2010 to provide a range of initiatives related to productivity enhancement and continuing education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: These include supporting productivity improvements for specific sectors and industries as well as developing infrastructure and tools to raise productivity across the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Productivity growth reduces production costs and increases returns on investments, some of which provide greater income for business owners and investors or enable businesses to pay their staff higher wages.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The amendment to this Bill is necessary as it provides greater flexibility with the usage of funds to build capabilities and anchor quality investments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As shared by Senior Minister of State Chee, I agree that investment is an important cornerstone of Singapore and I commend the Government's focus on developing the capability of our workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I believe skills development is central to improving productivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In turn, productivity is an important source of improved living standards and growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We also know that education, training and lifelong learning foster a cycle of higher productivity, more employment of better quality, income growth and development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I view skills development as crucial in improving productivity and fostering growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill aligns with SUSS' intention in developing capabilities to enhance workforce productivity and overall competitiveness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: While I acknowledge the potential benefits of this expansion, I have some minor concerns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is heartening to note from Senior Minister of State Chee the number of individuals who have benefited from CET.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, as we broaden the fund's usage, it is essential to ensure that the quantum allocated for CET is not reduced.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: At this juncture, I would like to clarify the measures in place to safeguard the use of funds for CET.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This will prevent the diversion of resources to other areas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, I am interested in understanding the mechanisms in place to monitor the return on investment from CET initiatives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As the nature of work evolves rapidly, we need to assess the effectiveness of CET programmes and their adaptability to the changing work landscape.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: A continuous and sustained approach is essential to support employees who may face job displacement due to technology and automation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: On that note, NPF supports the work of the 23 ITMs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Some of the larger projects funded by NPF include sector-specific schemes like the Construction Productivity and Capability Fund as well as schemes that support enterprise and workforce transformation like the Inclusive Growth Programme and the SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Projects supported by NPF complement our wider range of schemes and projects in driving productivity improvements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As we evolve, to ensure that no one is left behind, I believe we should also consider expanding the outreach of NPF to include sectors that engage gig economy workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: With the growth of digital platforms, the gig economy is booming, an ideal win-win situation for both the employers and jobseekers by providing a flexible workforce at a nominal cost to the employers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, the sustainability and employment prospects of gig workers are questionable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Is there any consideration given to how NPF could also extend and support the development and growth of gig workers?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I am concerned about equity in education for our workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Equity in education refers to ensuring that all individuals, regardless of their background or circumstances, have fair and equal access to educational opportunities, resources and support to develop their skills and reach their full potential.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It aims to remove barriers and disparities that may hinder certain groups from accessing quality education and training, thereby promoting a level playing field for everyone in the workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Inclusivity is vital in our approach to productivity enhancement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, as we focus on innovation and with the expansion arising from this Bill, I would like to suggest that we direct specific sectors, as they tap on the funds, to engage in R&D, specifically, in supporting initiatives like the Singapore Green Plan.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is crucial to maintain transparency and uphold high standards when it comes to the usage of the fund.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I trust that we have established guidelines to monitor the administrative aspects of fund allocation, particularly, in delivering CET programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Considering the fund will be used to anchor more quality investments in Singapore, I propose placing a stronger emphasis on the content and quality of the CET programmes offered.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: To achieve this, it is vital to establish oversight mechanisms that can effectively assess the excellence of these programmes and their impact on Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Skills development should be an integral part of our broader employment and development strategies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, I believe there is a strong correlation between the quality of CET programmes and improved job prospects for Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I appreciate the efforts to enhance the NPF and its administration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I believe this revision is a positive step towards advancing productivity and continuous learning in our nation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Members raised questions around three themes: one, adequacy of the NPF funds for various purposes; two, ensuring proper accountability and governance for NPF-funded projects; and three, providing support for specific groups or programmes through the NPF.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Assoc Prof Razwana asked whether part of the funds in the NPF could be ringfenced for CET and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim asked how we will ensure that NPF does not dilute its focus on productivity.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Foreign MNEs which invest in Singapore, bring with them new technologies, market access and business models which are internationally competitive.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The net injection of such companies raises the quality and productivity of our local economy.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Investments in CET build a skilled workforce, raising the overall productivity and competitiveness of our economy and enable our workers to earn higher wages over time.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: With a better skilled workforce, Singapore also becomes more attractive to foreign investments.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: MNEs in Singapore benefit the wider ecosystem as they provide valuable training to our workers or form partnerships with our local enterprises, including SMEs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The NPF is not the only source of funding for productivity enhancements, CET or investment promotion.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The NPF is generally used to fund new initiatives on productivity and CET.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Once these initiatives have proven to be effective, we will regularise them as mainstream programmes and they are then funded by the respective Ministries' annual budgets or other sources.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As for investment promotion, MTI will continue to tap on its annual budget for such activities.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, even as we expand the scope of supportable activities under the NPF to cover investment promotion, please let me assure Members that the Government will continue to set aside sufficient funding, be it in the NPF, Ministries' annual budgets or other funding sources, to support meritorious productivity enhancements, CET and investment promotion.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Sharael Taha asked about our ability to compete with other major jurisdictions for investments and what are the investments we are targeting.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Our intention is not to try and outbid the major economies in terms of overall spending.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: With limited resources, we cannot afford to do that.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In view of our constraints of land, labour and, increasingly carbon, we will have to play to our strengths and in areas where we have a competitive advantage.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Some are not compatible with Singapore's constraints and how we want to grow our economy.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This includes attracting foreign MNEs to make new significant investments here, to create good jobs in Singapore, provide training to our workers and partner our local enterprises.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: All these will be supplemented by a robust cost-benefit analysis to ensure that the value these MNEs bring to Singapore outweighs the incentives given to them.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Maybe he meant that in jest, because certainly that is not the plan.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As I mentioned in my opening speech, we want to target quality investments from MNEs to anchor those that can add value to Singapore, create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The broad phrasing in the Bill is to give flexibility, to be able to meet future needs and requirements, which can change over time.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But the intent is clear and I have said that clearly in my opening speech.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: At the same time, we will monitor the use of NPF funds across the three areas of productivity, CET and investment promotion.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It may not be meaningful to ringfence the funds for any specific area, since all three are mutually reinforcing.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Instead, we should preserve flexibility to accommodate fluctuations in spending from year to year, depending on factors, such as what the business needs are, what opportunities are available and what are the take-up rates of the various schemes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Assoc Prof Razwana mentioned that she was pleased to see the Bill will grant the Productivity Fund Administration Board, or PFAB, with the authority to inquire into and verify the accuracy of statements or information provided in applications for financing or incentives.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The PFAB already has the authority to verify the accuracy of statements made by applicants for a grant from the PFAB.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The intent of clause 4 is to clarify that the powers to obtain information under section 24 of the NPF Act apply not just to grants, but also to financing and incentives provided by the PFAB.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, this is an enhancement to an existing power of the PFAB.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Currently, NPF funds are channelled through Government agencies to support their productivity or CET schemes, and the individual agencies are responsible for the implementation of these schemes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As part of PFAB's governance process, implementing agencies must carry out regular internal audits and these audit reports will be submitted to the PFAB for review.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Rectifications will be made if there are audit observations raised.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The cases of fraud cited by Mr Sharael Taha pertain to the Productivity and Innovation Credit, or PIC, scheme.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Police investigated these cases and appropriate actions were taken against the perpetrators.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will adopt the same stringent approach for all funding sources to deter fraud and abuse cases.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In terms of monitoring of outcomes, we will monitor the progress of schemes funded by the NPF to see if they are on track to meeting their targets.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For a particular scheme, we also review its outcomes and assess whether it has met targets.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will then decide whether the scheme should be closed, extended or regularised as a steady state programme and funded from recurrent funding sources.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Sharael Taha asked how we can ensure that NPF funds contribute to productivity improvements that could lower the cost of doing business in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The NPF will continue to fund existing and new schemes to support our businesses to do so.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will also continually review the effectiveness of these schemes to ensure that they remain relevant and can help our firms to drive real productivity gains.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: One such example is the iSPRINT scheme, which supported SMEs to automate their business functions through information and communications technology (ICT).

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: A study by the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) found that the median firm saw an increase in revenue of 3.1% after adopting solutions under the iSPRINT scheme, compared to firms that had not adopted the solutions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: By and large, we have made good progress in driving productivity growth in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's comment that our labour productivity growth has been "anaemic", if I heard him correctly, is actually factually incorrect and is not supported by evidence.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Sharael Taha also asked for an update on the ITMs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I understand that MTI will provide a fuller update on this.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Third, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, Mr Sharael Taha and Assoc Prof Razwana gave several suggestions for NPF funds to be used to support specific programmes, like AI adoption as well as for specific worker segments, such as seniors and gig workers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Such efforts need not be and are not funded through the NPF alone.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Various Ministries and agencies contribute to these efforts through their budgets and other funding sources.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For instance, Assoc Prof Razwana suggested allowing firms to tap on NPF funds to engage in R&D.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I wish to inform Assoc Prof Razwana that firms can seek R&D funding through the $25 billion Research, Innovation and Enterprise (RIE) 2025 budget.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Sharael Taha and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim also suggested allowing firms to tap on NPF funds for AI adoption.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In fact, the Government has already been investing in AI, we have developed a national AI strategy and made significant R&D investments to build up our strengths and capabilities in AI.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have also rolled out programmes, like AI Singapore, to support enterprises to find suitable use cases and adopt AI.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As AI will affect each industry differently, economic agencies will have to develop tailored AI strategies on a sectorial basis and make plans for how to upskill and reskill our workers as jobs are transformed.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We are already funding these initiatives through the Ministries' annual budgets and other funds.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If need be, we can also use NPF funds to supplement this funding.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In short, if there are meritorious projects that are suitable for funding from the NPF, the PFAB will always welcome such proposals and Government agencies can submit them for funding consideration.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Through the expansion, we will continue to strengthen Singapore's proposition as a competitive and attractive place for business.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But even as we continue to compete for foreign investments, we will also keep our focus and continue investing in productivity and CET so that our local enterprises and workers can reap the full benefits from our investment promotion efforts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As I mentioned earlier, these areas are mutually reinforcing.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is how we can build a virtuous cycle for our economy to thrive through investment promotion where foreign MNEs want to set up in Singapore because they know we have strong local companies and a capable workforce supported by strong tripartite partnerships.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: At the same time, our local enterprises and our workers benefit from the MNEs' presence here, through access to valuable partnership opportunities and good jobs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The three pillars of our strategy are complementary and will help to grow our economy in a sustainable manner, for the benefit of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: First, let me start off by pointing out that while I understand the original intent of the Bill was along the lines, as Senior Minister of State Chee mentioned, which is, to promote both investment as well as productivity, my point when I gave those examples, which actually were not entirely in jest, was that the language leaves this door open for such alternative expenditures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, I am sure Senior Minister of State Chee will agree that precision in the language of the Bill is important, even as we wish to retain flexibility as much as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This will prevent the potential sort of abuses that one could imagine, perhaps in my somewhat ludicrous examples.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: On the issue of productivity, I do not want to get too much into the weeds, but there are two distinct measures of productivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: One is, as Senior Minister of State Chee mentioned, labour productivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But, in fact, there is another measure which is more precise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is productivity after you take into account all the observable factors of production, and here, unfortunately, I would take issue with the fact that the evidence is incorrect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In fact, I mentioned that in the 1960s through to the 1990s, evidence is abundant in this regard.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The first evidence came from Alwyn Young, an economist that was currently at the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE) at the time at Chicago.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It has been corroborated by other economists, Chang-Tai Hsieh in 2002, using a different methodology, came up with the continued finding that productivity in Singapore remains low.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: More recently, MTI did have a publication in 2010 where they looked at the measure and MTI tends to have the highest numbers, but other authors, like Bhaskaran and Chiang in 2020, continued to find that Singapore has poor productivity performance, even as recently as the 2010s.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, unfortunately, I am sure we can continue to disagree, but the point is that there is a slate of evidence, not just drawn from my own research but from other academics, that demonstrates that Singapore's total factor productivity, after you take into account observable factors of production, remains and I did use this word "anaemic".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Just one final point, Mr Speaker, I do, in fact, despite my reservations, support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I was not sure whether he supported the Bill, that was why I was careful in how I phrased it.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I mentioned it earlier in my response speech.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I hope that gives assurance to Assoc Prof Lim.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: On the point about productivity, Sir, I know there is a range of different reports with different figures – maybe because they make different assumptions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Like Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, I do not want to go into a lengthy debate here.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I think these are proof points that matter most, I think, to Singapore, to our companies and to our workers.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Any other clarifications for Senior Minister of State Chee?
